newsitem.title: CANADA: Royal Bank Canada arranges C$3 bln financing.
newsitem.headline: Royal Bank Canada arranges C$3 bln financing.

text.p: Royal Bank of Canada said on Friday that it will arrange C$3 billion in financing for Nav Canada 's acquisition of the Canadian civil air navigation system from the Canadian government.
The three-tranche facility will provide the initial funding for the acquisition until Nav Canada phases in its capital markets financing, the bank said.

Some of the financing arranged by the bank will cover Nav Canada's day-to-day needs after the acquisition is completed. Nav Canada is a non-share capital corporation with exclusive rights to Canada's air traffic operations.
Royal Bank said the financing was divided into two Canadian domestic tranches of between C$750 million and C$1 billion each and an international tranche of between C$1 billion and C$1.5 billion.
The total financing would not exceed C$3 billion, the bank said.

The domestic tranches will be revolving with maturities of 30 months and five years respectively, with the international tranche having an initial availability of 364 days with a five-year term out. The pricing is governed by a six-part grid reflecting the rating of Nav Canada.
As a non-share capital corporation, Nav Canada has members, rather than shareholders or other equity holders.

One member is appointed by the Canadian government, two by user groups representing commercial air carriers and business aircraft operators and one by unions representing the company's employees. Other aviation interests are represented by 126 non-voting associate members. The acquisition is expected to close in October. Nav Canada will have more than 6,000 employees operating from seven area control centers, two terminal control units, 44 control towers and 86 flight services stations in Canada.
Nav Canada will be able to levy user fees for its services to meet its current and future financial requirements, such as debt service and reserves for future expenditures and contingencies.

The company will move to fund its operations entirely through user fees within the first two years of closing of the acquisition. During this transition period the Canadian government will pay the company up to C$1.44 billion in revenues it collects through the present Air Transport Tax to supplement the user fee structure being implemented.
